thread.title: Why Index Investing Could Miss the Best Stock Bets

author: Evie Liu
title: Why Index Investing Could Miss the Best Stock Bets
text:
By Evie Liu Aug. 16, 2018 5:35 p.m. ET Since the introduction of index funds and emergence of exchange-traded funds in the 1990s, more and more money has been flowing into these passive products from active managers.
According to the Investment Company Institute , U.S. equity mutual funds lost $108 billion in 2018, while ETFs added $37 billion in assets. Today, there are more indexes in the U.S. than there are stocks, according to estimates from research and brokerage firm Sanford C. Bernstein .
Throughout the steady, peaceful bull run over the past decade, passive funds–which often feature relatively low fees–have topped active managers. Last year, The Wall Street Journal noted that more than 90% of active managers underperformed their benchmark indexes over a 15-year period. But a comeback could be in the offing for active managers amid higher market volatility and ongoing geopolitical risks.
Vincent Deluard , a global macro strategist at INTL FCStone , suggests that identifying and investing in individual gems could outperform owning entire indexes, moving forward.
According to Deluard, popular stocks that are featured in more indexes are generally more expensive, and their performances are starting to disappoint due to overvaluation.
Stocks within the Russell 3000 that are featured in more than 200 indexes have an average price-to-book ratio of 3.67, while those included in fewer than 75 indexes only trade at 1.75 times book value. It's important to note that correlation does not equal causation. It's difficult to parse out whether more exposure in indexes is driving up the valuation of popular stocks, or, conversely, that indexes prefer picking well-performing stocks as components.
However, that might not matter anymore, as the stocks underrepresented by indexes are surging as of late. Despite underperforming on a five-year basis, stocks included in fewer than 75 indexes have achieved a much higher return over the latest 12 months than all the other stocks - 62% up, to be exact.
The comeback of small caps this year may have contributed to that rebound, as larger stocks with higher market capitalizations tend to appear more in indexes, according to Deluard. Since many index providers charge fees based on the assets benchmarked against their indexes, they have an incentive to include larger stocks that can bring in higher fees. Apple (AAPL), for example, is featured in at least 207 indexes.
But size might not be the only reason, as the same trend was found in another group of "index dropouts" that all fall into the large-cap category. We know that in order to be included in the S&P 500 index, a company must meet criteria beyond the size requirement. According to Deluard's analysis, large stocks excluded by the Standard & Poor’s committee for failing other criteria–although lagging the S&P 500 index by 50% since 1995–have actually slightly outperformed the index since January 2016.
It might be time to give dropouts another chance.
